Sensitivity to a biased search

Source: R/sens_bias.R
sens_bias.Rd

The paper's rule sets the rival aside, at least provisionally, when the uniform-weights Bayes factor is 20 or more and the worst-case Bayes factor is above 1. A reader who doubts the result may ask whether the search for evidence favored the working theory. Write \(\omega\) for the bias factor: a search with bias \(\omega\) is \(\omega\) times as likely to find a pro-working-theory observation as a pro-rival one. Granting more bias lowers both Bayes factors, because a search that finds pro-working-theory observations more easily would produce mostly pro-working-theory counts even from evidence that mostly favored the rival.

Usage

sens_bias(y_W, y_R, threshold_uniform = 20, threshold_worst = 1)

Arguments

y_W

Non-negative whole number. Count, or summed weight, of observations supporting the working theory.

y_R

Non-negative whole number. Count, or summed weight, of observations supporting the rival.

threshold_uniform

Positive number. The uniform-weights Bayes factor must be at least this large for the rule to set the rival aside. Default 20.

threshold_worst

Positive number. The worst-case Bayes factor must be above this value for the rule to set the rival aside. Default 1.

Value

A list with elements

bf_uniform, bf_worst

The two Bayes factors at an unbiased search.

omega_uniform

The bias at which the uniform-weights Bayes factor falls to threshold_uniform.

omega_worst

The bias at which the worst-case Bayes factor falls to threshold_worst.

omega_star

The smaller of the two.

Details

This function returns the bias at which each condition of the rule fails and the smaller of the two, which the paper writes \(\omega^\star\): the smallest bias at which a researcher following the rule would no longer set the rival aside. At nine observations for the working theory and three for the rival, the uniform-weights value falls to 20 at a bias of 1.0098 and the worst-case value falls to 1 at 1.559, so \(\omega^\star = 1.01\): a search about one percent more likely to find pro-working-theory observations would change the decision. With the smoking-gun memo counted as ten observations, the counts are 18 and 3 and \(\omega^\star = 2.33\).

Whether a search could have been that lopsided is a question about how the evidence was collected, which readers who know the case can answer and the function cannot.

Special values

A tipping point is 0 when its condition already fails at an unbiased search, because then there is no decision for bias to change. It is Inf when no bias makes the condition fail: with no observations for the rival, both Bayes factors fall toward 1 as the bias grows and never reach it, so a threshold of 1 or less is never crossed. It is NA when the search, which tries biases up to about \(10^{12}\), finds no crossing; omega_star then reports the other tipping point.

See also

bf_uniform_weights() and bf_worst_case(), whose omega argument this function varies; sens_coding() for sensitivity to coding.

Examples

# The paper's running example.
sens_bias(9, 3)
#> $bf_uniform
#> [1] 20.67196
#> 
#> $bf_worst
#> [1] 2.732168
#> 
#> $omega_uniform
#> [1] 1.009794
#> 
#> $omega_worst
#> [1] 1.559262
#> 
#> $omega_star
#> [1] 1.009794
#> 

# The memo counted as ten observations.
sens_bias(18, 3)$omega_star
#> [1] 2.334075
